phase.label: Last years, President of the Board of Rites (1630s)

source.label: Sirén (citing the Wusheng shi shi): in the Chongzhen reign (1628–44) he was made president of the Board of Rites
Metropolitan Museum of Art: a poem written out by Dong Qichang

work.text: Painting and calligraphy both [have] their special characteristics. Calligraphy should be fresh …, but painting should be ripe

source.author: Dong Qichang (Tung Ch‘i-ch‘ang)
source.title: Writings on painting
source.publisher: translated in Osvald Sirén, Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V (Lund Humphries, 1958; Internet Archive scan)

work.text: This rank is given to Tung out of respect for his wonderful talents as a [calligraphist] in which he stands among the great masters. He could write in any of the three styles—regular, running, or draft.
work.lead: Ferguson on why Dong ranks among the great Ming masters:

source.author: John C. Ferguson
source.title: Chinese Painting
source.publisher: University of Chicago Press (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: In calligraphy it is possible to create new styles; but in painting the familiar is essential.

source.author: Dong Qichang (Tung Ch‘i-ch‘ang)
source.title: Writings on painting
source.publisher: translated in Arthur Waley, An Introduction to the Study of Chinese Painting (Ernest Benn, 1923; Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: Even emperors, high officials, district magistrates, and provincial [governors] applied to him for help in writing letters and farewell messages, which he could do better than anybody else.

source.author: Jiang Shaoshu (Chiang Shao-shu)
source.title: Wusheng shi shi (biography of Dong Qichang)
source.publisher: translated in Osvald Sirén, Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V (Lund Humphries, 1958; Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: Still, when approaching the age of [80], he could read by lamplight books with characters no larger than a fly's head, and write equally small characters.
